title: My Five Most Interesting Trends From the NBA’s First Month

 The NBA has a new king of the lob. Plus, can the Sixers win big with this version of Joel Embiid? Getty Images/Ringer illustration By Kirk Goldsberry Nov. 17, 2:13 pm UTC • 7 min The NBA season is only a month old, but we’re already seeing some emerging trends that will shape the rest of the campaign. I pored over the data so you don’t have to, and here are the five most interesting trends that stood out to me. 
 The Spurs are the new kings of the lob.
 After starting the season 0-2, San Antonio has now won 12 straight games, the organization’s longest winning streak in over a decade and a dominant stretch that has San Antonio tied for the best record in the NBA. How are they doing it? Let’s start with the lobs. 
 No team in league history has been this good at them. It’s no secret why: The Spurs offense is built around the best alley-oop target in NBA history. Victor Wembanyama is impossible to defend. He’s dunking the ball at a rate we’ve never seen , and lobs are a huge part of how he gets so many looks at the rim. 
 Coming into this season, no team in the player-tracking era (since 2013-14) had ever averaged over three converted lobs per contest. This year’s Spurs are averaging 4.4 per game! I know what you’re thinking: What about those old Clippers teams with prime Chris Paul and two monster frontcourt athletes in DeAndre Jordan and Blake Griffin? After all, their team was literally nicknamed “Lob City.” Well, look at this.
 Those Clippers teams never averaged more than 2.3 made lobs per game; the Spurs surpassed that figure last season and now are nearly doubling it. This isn’t just because of Wembanyama. San Antonio has three great attacking guards in its rotation, and Stephon Castle and De’Aaron Fox in particular are adept at the launch of the lob. Zoom out, and the league’s top two lob duos are both wearing silver and black. 
 Notice that Dylan Harper is not listed here. Well, he has a different approach at the cup—he finishes at elite rates all by himself, no lobs needed. 
 The Spurs’ second-year phenom is out here making the leap in real time. His scoring is up from 11.8 points per game to 18.3, and at age 20, Harper is already the best finishing guard in the NBA. Here are the receipts: Out of the 24 players who have taken at least 50 shots in the restricted area so far this season, Wembanyama is the most efficient, at 82 percent. Harper ranks second, at 80 percent. He is also the only first- or second-year player currently averaging over 10 points per game in the paint. Not bad for a guard.
 If you want to be the first team to beat San Antonio in three-plus weeks, all you have to do is stop these dudes at the rim. 
 Joel Embiid is in decline.
 The Sixers have a lot to be happy about. They are 12-3 and neck-and-neck with the Celtics at the top of the East; however, there is one giant red flag, and he wears no. 21. 
 Embiid is off to a bad start, and that may be an understatement. Among all players who have tried at least 100 shots this season, Embiid ranks last in points per shot—143rd out of 143. Through Sunday’s games, Embiid had made 61 of his 163 field goal attempts. For those of us who have studied Embiid’s stats for years, that number is downright alarming. 
 The eye test doesn’t look much better. In a few of his most recent appearances, Embiid has had some really scary moments . 
 The worst part is that the arrivals of LeBron James and Jaylen Brown were supposed to help Embiid downshift to another phase of his career. Generally speaking, we expect lower usage to lead to increased or at least steady efficiency, but not here. As Embiid’s offensive burden has been reduced, his points per shot has cratered too. 
 The problems go deeper than just shooting. Embiid’s usage is down. His assists are down. He is averaging just 1.1 blocks and 10.6 free throw attempts per 100 possessions, both the lowest of his career. He’s no longer protecting the rim or getting to the line.
 Embiid won NBA MVP four years ago. He will turn 33 in March. Philadelphia’s big man is currently signed to a three-year, $188 million deal that extends through the 2028-29 season (including a $67.3 million player option in the final year). 
 There's no doubt that the beginning of the 2026-27 season has been one of the roughest on-court stretches of Embiid's NBA career, but all is not lost. He's now surrounded by the deepest supporting cast of his Philly tenure, and he just played the best game of his season so far, scoring 32 points on 22 shots in the Sixers’ win over Brooklyn on Monday night. It could be a turning point, or it could be an anomaly. The supporting cast will help the Sixers win regular-season games even if Embiid is in decline, but this roster wasn't built for the regular season.
 Boston’s defense hasn’t missed a beat.
 The Celtics have been one of the hottest teams in the East, and their league-leading interior defense is a major reason. They are allowing just 34.9 paint points per game, the fewest in the league and on pace to be the lowest such number this decade. Boston has gone full Budenholzer on defense, protecting the rim at all costs and daring opponents to beat them from deep. Celtics opponents are launching 43 3s per game while attempting a league-low 34.9 shots in the paint. 
 That interior suppression starts with some of the best on-ball perimeter defenders in the league. Specifically, Paul George and Derrick White give Boston’s starting group two excellent wing defenders, while Jordan Walsh and Baylor Scheierman provide Boston with even more defensive depth on the edges. All told, the Celtics can reliably switch assignments, and their length at every position makes them a pain to attack. 
 Boston’s five-point win in Toronto last week was a perfect example. The Celtics held the Raptors to 20 points in the paint—the lowest such output by any team thus far this season. Then, as they drubbed the Mavs on Sunday, Boston held Dallas to just 32 points in the lane. 
 When most people think of Mazzulla Ball, they think of a five-out offense with smart passing and endless 3s, but this level of paint protection is also a signature element; Boston led the league in this category last season, as well. 
 Luka Doncic is going for broke.
 Is Doncic playing the best basketball of his career? It sure looks like it. The Lakers are 12-2 and have the best offense in the NBA, and Doncic is the biggest reason for both. He currently leads the whole league in usage rate, scoring, 3-pointers made, and free throws made. 
 Despite the fact that he’s taking an absurd 25 shots per game, he’s somehow also on pace to set a new career best in effective field goal percentage, at 59.6 percent!
 It all adds up to perhaps the most ludicrous stat of the young season. Doncic is averaging 39 points per game, a level no player has sustained for a full season since Wilt Chamberlain averaged 44.8 in 1962-63.
 That mind-blowing production is being driven by his improved numbers downtown, where the Slovenian superstar is converting a ridiculous 40.6 percent of his 13.3 3-point attempts per contest. That figure would be elite for any shooter in the league, but it’s particularly stunning when you consider that Luka creates the vast majority of his own 3-pointers off the bounce. So far, only 33.8 percent of his made 3s have involved an assist. That’s a pretty different formula from Wilt’s. 
 Doncic’s signature weapon is obviously his stepback triple. As of Monday, he’s already made 37 stepback 3s this season, more than twice as many as Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who ranks second with 18.
 This shot is becoming so unstoppable that it demands a nickname. Jokic has the Sombor Shuffle; what can we call this? The Slovenian Slither? If Doncic can stay healthy and his shooting numbers can remain this efficient, the Lakers will be a factor in the West all season long.

 Along with the Lakers, the Rockets, Grizzlies, and Blazers are also outperforming preseason expectations. While many of us thought the Eastern Conference would be the superior half of the league this season, it hasn’t happened. 
 The West is crushing. West teams are 32-13 in head-to-head games against East teams, winning by 7.62 points on average. 
 So far this season, six of the league’s top seven teams by net rating play in the West. The exception is the Celtics, but outside of them, the East’s supposed contenders have been mediocre. The Knicks are 7-6. Cleveland is 7-7 with the league’s 21st-ranked defense. Miami is 7-6 with a negative net rating. Orlando is 5-7, and Indiana, the 2025 conference champ, is once again missing Tyrese Haliburton and sits at just 5-9. 
 This isn’t new, even if it is unexpected. Going back to 1999-2000, the West has had a winning record vs. the East in 24 of 27 seasons. Looks like it will be 25 of 28 by mid-April. 
 Stats updated through Sunday’s games.
